Flash remediation — Phase 1: what is the flash, and what causes it?

FoV-truncation artifacts in mbirjax MBIR recon · 2026-07-08 · plan of record: plans/flash_remediation/flash_remediation_plan.md · the remediation A/Bs built on these results: phase_2a_axial_results.html · scripts: plans/experiments/flash_remediation/

TL;DR. Both flash artifacts (the radial ring and the SiC-like axial flash + z-ringing) reproduce on small synthetic cone-beam cases, and both are confirmed to be model-support problems: enlarging the reconstruction support with the existing scale_recon_shape() essentially eliminates them.

Radial (object wider than the FoV): padding improves the RoR-edge ring 37× and the interior 2.8× — lateral truncation biases the entire interior, which no channel weight taper can reach.

Axial, one-sided (object taller than the covered slab): padding improves the truncated-end slices 9× and removes the z-ringing; the artifact is localized, and grows with iterations if unaddressed.

1  The two truncation cases at a glance

MBIR explains the measured attenuation with the voxels of the reconstruction support. When part of the scanned object lies outside that support, the data term is inconsistent: some measured attenuation has no voxels that can account for it. The optimizer deposits that unexplained attenuation in the least-constrained voxels available — the ones at the support boundary — producing the bright “flash.” The two ways an object can leave the support behave differently, and the distinction drives the remediation choice.

Radial (channel) truncation — top view

The object is wider than the FoV. As the gantry rotates, material at radius r beyond the FoV sweeps across every channel |c| ≤ r — the inconsistency lands throughout the sinogram, not just at the edge channels. Artifact: bright ring at the RoR boundary plus a positive bias over the whole interior. Seen in: z62 (partition study), the BGA scan. §3 below.

Axial (row) truncation — side view

The object extends past the covered slab in z (here one-sided, like SiC). Rays reaching the edge detector rows traverse slices above the recon slab — that data is locally unexplainable, and nothing else in the sinogram is touched. Artifact: flash + damped ringing confined to the truncated end; the interior is unaffected. Seen in: the SiC composite scan. §4 below. Drawing note: the object is centered on the rotation axis (through the middle of the dashed support, as in §4), and the support's corners on the source side poke outside this view's cone deliberately — the support is the region covered in at least one view, and those corners are covered once the gantry has rotated 180°.

The asymmetry matters for remediation: the radial case corrupts the whole volume through interior channels, so down-weighting edge channels cannot fix it — enlarging the support can. The axial case is local and mirrors the situation the split_sino_recon sine weight taper already handles at an artificial detector-row split, so there a zero-memory row taper looked like a credible alternative to padding. (Phase 2 measured that head-to-head; see phase_2a_axial_results.html for how it came out.)

2  Method

Each case builds the ground truth phantom on an enlarged recon grid attached to a model that shares the real (small) detector. Forward-projecting that grid through the real detector is the physical truncated measurement — no sinogram cropping or other surgery, so the data inconsistency is exactly the one a real scan produces. Reconstruction then runs on the default-shape model (what a user gets: recon width = detector FoV at iso, zero margin), one iteration at a time, with per-region error tracked against the aligned center crop of the ground truth phantom.

  • Geometry: cone beam, magnification 2, 128 views over 2π, 40 iterations, default reconstruction parameters, unit weights.
  • Variants: default (auto recon shape) vs padded (scale_recon_shape, support enlarged to cover the object; recon compared on the same cropped voxels).
  • Regions: interior (r < 0.85 R, central slices), ring (0.85 R–R annulus inside the RoR), end slices (top / bottom slabs). NRMSE is normalized by the ground-truth RMS over the RoR cylinder, so values are comparable across regions. Each montage below outlines its metric's region on the truth panel and carries the per-recon value in the panel title.

3  Radial (lateral) truncation — the ring

Phantom: a cylinder of radius 1.25× the FoV radius (contained in z), with three embedded spheres. Default grid (128, 128, 32); ground truth phantom (172, 172, 32); padded variant ×1.35 laterally → (172, 172, 32).

What the reconstructions look like

The radial profile

Convergence, and the numbers

Variant (iter 40)interior NRMSEring NRMSEring excess (signed)
default0.2252.21+0.028
padded ×1.350.0810.060+0.0004

What this settles

Material outside the FoV projects onto interior channels too (a point at radius r crosses every channel |c| ≤ r as views rotate), so the inconsistency is spread across the sinogram and the whole interior pays. A channel weight taper can only address the edge channels — it cannot reach the interior bias — while support padding attacks the cause and fixes both. For the lateral case the open question is only the padding cost knee (memory ~scale²), not whether it is the right lever.

4  Axial truncation, one-sided — flash + z-ringing (the SiC case)

Phantom: a laminated cylinder (radius 0.75× FoV, alternating ±20% layers, one embedded sphere) whose bottom ends inside the covered slab but whose top extends 60% of a half-slab beyond it — like the SiC composite, which stays inside the FoV in channels but leaves the detector in rows. Default grid (96, 96, 64); ground truth phantom (96, 96, 116); padded variant ×1.7 in z → (96, 96, 108).

Variant (iter 40)interior NRMSEtruncated-end NRMSEcontained-end NRMSE
default0.04720.6190.0433

What this settles

Unlike the lateral case, the axial artifact is local: the interior is untouched, and only the rows/slices near the truncated end are involved. That makes it exactly the situation the split_sino_recon sine taper already handles at an artificial split — so a geometry-derived row taper (zero memory cost) looked like a credible competitor to z-padding here. That head-to-head became Phase 2's first experiment (P2a), and padding won it decisively — see phase_2a_axial_results.html.

5  What Phase 1 set up

  • Padding is the standard to beat in both axes. Any weight-taper candidate must be A/B'd against scale_recon_shape on the same case — the Phase 2 program does exactly that, per axis.
  • Channels: a taper cannot fix the interior bias (mechanism, confirmed visually); the useful sweep is the padding scale knee versus its ~scale² memory cost (Phase 2's P2b).
  • Rows: the taper-vs-padding head-to-head (Phase 2's P2a — since run: padding won, and the row taper is retired for the axial case).
  • Stop-metric interaction: the flash region is what keeps converging (slowly) while it also drags the change-% metric — remediation should both improve quality and let the 0.2% stop fire honestly.
  • Caveat: the "slower convergence" field observation only partially reproduced on these simple phantoms (damage was mostly a fast-reached bias floor). Watch for it on structured/real data in Phase 3 (SiC, z62, BGA).

6  Reproduction

Scripts: plans/experiments/flash_remediation/lateral_truncation_repro.py and z_truncation_repro.py (shared machinery in truncation_common.py); all knobs at the top of each script, no CLI args. Each runs in a few minutes on local CPU in the mbirjax conda env and writes these figures to figures/ plus metrics/recons to results/. Figures in this page are embedded (the repo gitignores PNGs); refresh them with embed_report_figures.py after a rerun.
